claims.claim: David Hartlage dates the introduction of boxed text descriptions read by the DM on entry to Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan in 1979.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text', DMDavid, 2012
claims.quote: In 1979, Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan introduced boxed text descriptions

claims.claim: David Hartlage attributes the original purpose of boxed text to giving every table the same play experience in tournament competition.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text', DMDavid, 2012
claims.quote: a consistent play experience in a competitive environment

claims.claim: David Hartlage reports that in a tournament the significant detail was placed among less important ones in the boxed text and his team missed it.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text', DMDavid, 2012
claims.quote: the text mentioned the runes alongside other, less important details

claims.claim: David Hartlage says a reader's voice takes a different tone and cadence from extemporaneous speech, and that monotony lets players' attention wander.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text', DMDavid, 2012
claims.quote: their voice takes a different tone and cadence

claims.claim: David Hartlage defends boxed text as still the best available summary of what players must learn on entering a room.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text', DMDavid, 2012
claims.quote: No one has shown a better way to summarize

claims.claim: David Hartlage says that when he knows the material well he paraphrases the boxed text rather than reading it.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text', DMDavid, 2012

claims.claim: David Noonan reports that from watching Gen Con 2005 tables a DM reading aloud holds attention for two sentences.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: If you’re the DM, you get two sentences. Period.

claims.claim: The same Wizards article labels its own Gen Con observation qualitative rather than a controlled measurement.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: this kind of “research” is pretty qualitative
claims.page: Here's the Plan: We're Going Undercover!

claims.claim: David Noonan's explanation for the attention loss is that boxed text substitutes oration for the conversation that a game normally is.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: Boxed text replaces that conversation with oration.

claims.claim: David Noonan describes a D&D game as at heart a conversation between the DM and the players.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: At its heart, a D&D game is a conversation.

claims.claim: David Noonan's prior hypothesis, which the watching exceeded, was that boxed text longer than a paragraph is not worth reading.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: boxed text longer than a paragraph probably isn’t worth reading

claims.claim: Writing for Wizards of the Coast in 2005, David Noonan advises DMs to ditch the boxed text and describe the room in their own words.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: ditch the boxed text and use your own words
claims.page: Beyond the door, you see a format change

claims.claim: David Noonan observes that boxed text in Wizards adventures had become markedly shorter by 2005 than in earlier products.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: Boxed text in adventures used to be a lot longer

claims.claim: James Maliszewski reports that Gygax attributed his own voice to the old fashioned books he read as a boy rather than to Jack Vance.

claims.claim: In the same account Gygax credited a lifelong love of dictionaries and thesauruses for his vocabulary.

claims.quote: his lifelong love of dictionaries and thesauruses

verdicts.note: Raw dmdavid.com tag page (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200) carries the whole 15 Nov 2012 post by David Hartlage. Sentence appears in full: 'In 1979, Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan introduced boxed text descriptions for the DM to read when the players entered a location.' Every limb (1979, that module, DM reads on entry) supported.

Verbatim: 'The boxed text provided a way to offer a consistent play experience in a competitive environment.' Tournament limb supported by the preceding sentence (Origins '79 Official AD&D tournament) and by 'its original purpose of leveling a competition'; 'every table the same' supported by 'every team heard the same boxed text'.

Verbatim: 'Like any good boxed text description, the text mentioned the runes alongside other, less important details.' Tournament limb = 2012 GEN CON D&D Championship final; missed limb = 'No one on my team appreciated the runes significance, so we failed to discover...'.

Verbatim in the full sentence: 'When most speakers read something aloud, their voice takes a different tone and cadence than when they speak extemporaneously, and that monotony can cause players' attention to wander.' Both limbs supported.

Verbatim: 'No one has shown a better way to summarize what the players must learn when they enter a room.' Preceded by 'Still, even for DMs who never read boxed text, it helps', which supports the 'defends ... still the best available' framing.
Verbatim inside 'For this reason, when I know the content well enough, I paraphrase boxed text.' Knowledge-conditional limb supported by 'when I know the content well enough'.

Wayback capture 20161031220137 of archive.wizards.com fetched raw (HTTP 200). Verbatim: 'If you're the DM, you get two sentences. Period. Beyond that, your players are stacking dice, talking to each other, or staring off into space.' Gen Con 2005 limb supported ('went to Indianapolis for Gen Con 2005'); the first-person observer is Dave/David Noonan ('the "Dave wanders around" technique'; About the Authors: Design: David Noonan).

Verbatim: 'this kind of "research" is pretty qualitative, which is science-speak for "quite possibly bogus."' The 'not a controlled measurement' limb is supported by the next sentence: 'The "Dave wanders around" technique is no way to get a representative sample'.

Verbatim: 'Boxed text replaces that conversation with oration. Now the DM is doing the talking, and the players are doing the listening.' Framed by 'I started to develop a working theory for why listening comprehension takes a dive', so 'his explanation for the attention loss' is supported; the page itself ranks it above the two other factors ('the conversation vs. oration factor').

Verbatim: 'At its heart, a D&D game is a conversation.' The DM/players limb is supported by the following example: 'You tell the DM what you want to do, and the DM replies with the consequences of the action.'

Verbatim: 'My hypothesis was that boxed text longer than a paragraph probably isn't worth reading, because players tend to have pretty bad listening comprehension.' The 'which the watching exceeded' limb is supported by the next paragraph's opener: 'What I actually saw was much more dramatic than my hypothesis.'

Verbatim: 'Or better yet, ditch the boxed text and use your own words for the initial description of the room.' Advice-to-DMs limb explicit ('if you're the DM'); dated 09/16/2005 in the Wizards Design & Development header.

Verbatim in the Tangent Alert: 'Boxed text in adventures used to be a lot longer than it is today.' The 'Wizards adventures' limb is carried by the two examples contrasted - the short passage from the recent WotC Forgotten Realms adventure Sons of Gruumsh against the long one from 1999's Return to the Keep on the Borderlands; 'by 2005' = the article's 'today'.

Raw grognardia.blogspot.com post (curl, HTTP 200), 19 Feb 2009. Verbatim quoted phrase inside: 'saying that it was mostly the result of his having read a lot of rather "old fashioned" books when he was a kid'. The 'rather than to Jack Vance' limb is supported by the two preceding sentences: 'I once told Gary my opinion on this and he demurred. He didn't think his own peculiar voice was anywhere as erudite and witty as that of Jack Vance.' Private-conversation framing supported by 'I once told Gary'.

verdicts.trueWording: credited for his peculiar voice, not 'vocabulary' as such
verdicts.note: Same sentence, same account: '...coupled with his lifelong love of dictionaries and thesauruses' - quoted phrase is word for word. Graded SUBSTANCE rather than VERBATIM because what Gygax is reported to have credited is 'his own peculiar voice' (his style/diction), not 'his vocabulary' - the page's only 'vocabulary' sentences are Maliszewski's own ('my vocabulary grew considerably') and commenters'. The reported cause is also joint (old-fashioned books plus the dictionary/thesaurus love), where the claim names only the second.
